option_d: For a period of 10 years
explanation: According to DORA Art. 54(6), the publication of the decision imposing the administrative penalty shall remain on the authority's official website only for the period which is necessary to bring forth this Article, which shall not exceed five years after its publication.

scenario: A bank in Germany receives confidential information from a regulatory authority in the EU.
question: What is the nature of the confidential information received by the bank?
option_a: Publicly available information
option_b: Information covered by professional secrecy
option_c: Information that can be disclosed to any other person or authority
option_d: Information that is not subject to any secrecy requirements
explanation: According to DORA Art. 55.1, any confidential information received, exchanged or transmitted pursuant to this Regulation shall be subject to the conditions of professional secrecy laid down in paragraph 2.

scenario: A financial institution in France is considering disclosing confidential information to a third-party auditor.
question: What condition must be met before disclosing the information?
option_a: The auditor is a member of the EU's financial regulatory body
option_b: The auditor is contracted by the financial institution
option_c: The auditor is a natural or legal person to whom the regulatory authority has delegated their powers
option_d: The information is publicly available
explanation: According to DORA Art. 55.2, the obligation of professional secrecy applies to all persons who work, or who have worked, for the competent authorities pursuant to this Regulation, or for any authority or market undertaking or natural or legal person to whom those competent authorities have delegated their powers, including auditors and experts contracted by them.

scenario: A European Supervisory Authority in Germany needs to process personal data for an ongoing investigation.
question: What is the maximum period for retaining personal data under DORA?
option_a: 5 years
option_b: 15 years
option_c: 10 years
option_d: 20 years
explanation: According to DORA Art. 56, the personal data shall be retained for a maximum period of 15 years.

scenario: A financial institution in France wants to process personal data for communication purposes.
question: What regulation must the financial institution follow when processing personal data?
option_a: Regulation (EU) 2015/2015
option_b: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 or Regulation (EU) 2018/1725
option_c: Regulation (EU) 2017/2017
option_d: Regulation (EU) 2019/2019
explanation: According to DORA Art. 56, the personal data shall be processed in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 or Regulation (EU) 2018/1725, whichever is applicable.

scenario: A small business in Germany is implementing a data protection policy.
question: What is the primary objective of GDPR?
option_a: To protect the free movement of personal data within the EU
option_b: To protect fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons and their right to the protection of personal data
option_c: To promote the use of personal data for commercial purposes
option_d: To restrict the free movement of personal data within the EU
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 1(2), the Regulation protects fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons and in particular their right to the protection of personal data.

scenario: A French company is considering restricting the free movement of personal data within the EU.
question: What should the company consider when restricting the free movement of personal data?
option_a: Reasons connected with the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and national security
option_b: Reasons connected with the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data
option_c: Reasons connected with the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and economic growth
option_d: Reasons connected with the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and public health
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 1(3), the free movement of personal data within the Union shall be neither restricted nor prohibited for reasons connected with the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data.

scenario: A private company in Germany is wondering if GDPR applies to its data processing activities.
question: What type of activities does GDPR not apply to?
option_a: Activities related to the prevention of cybercrime
option_b: Activities which fall outside the scope of Union law
option_c: Activities carried out by a sole proprietorship
option_d: Activities related to the execution of criminal penalties
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 2(a), this Regulation does not apply to the processing of personal data in the course of an activity which falls outside the scope of Union law.

scenario: A public institution in France wants to know what type of data is covered by GDPR.
question: What type of data is covered by GDPR?
option_a: Data processed by a natural person in the course of a purely personal or household activity
option_b: Data processed wholly or partly by automated means
option_c: Data processed by the Member States when carrying out activities which fall within the scope of Chapter 3 of Title V of the TEU
option_d: Data processed by a natural person in the course of a purely commercial activity
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 2(1), this Regulation applies to the processing of personal data wholly or partly by automated means and to the processing other than by automated means of personal data which form part of a filing system or are intended to form part of a filing system.

scenario: A company in France is offering goods to customers in the EU.
question: What is the territorial scope of GDPR for this company?
option_a: The company must comply with the GDPR only if the processing takes place in the EU.
option_b: The company must comply with the GDPR regardless of whether the processing takes place in the EU or not.
option_c: The company must comply with the GDPR only if the customers are in France.
option_d: The company must comply with the GDPR if the customers are in the UK.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 3.1, the Regulation applies to the processing of personal data in the context of the activities of an establishment of a controller or a processor in the Union, regardless of whether the processing takes place in the Union or not.

scenario: A US company is monitoring the behaviour of users in the EU.
question: What is the condition under which the GDPR applies to this US company?
option_a: The company must be established in the EU.
option_b: The company must be offering goods or services to users in the EU.
option_c: The company must be monitoring the behaviour of users in the US.
option_d: The company must be monitoring the behaviour of users in the UK.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 3.2(a), the Regulation applies to the processing of personal data of data subjects who are in the Union by a controller or processor not established in the Union, where the processing activities are related to the offering of goods or services, irrespective of whether a payment of the data subject is required, to such data subjects in the Union.

scenario: A small business in Germany needs to ensure compliance with GDPR principles.
question: What is required of the controller under GDPR Art. 5?
option_a: To store personal data for up to 10 years.
option_b: To be responsible for and be able to demonstrate compliance with paragraph 1.
option_c: To process personal data in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the data, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing.
option_d: To keep personal data in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 5(2), the controller shall be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with, paragraph 1.

scenario: A startup in France wants to use customer data for a new marketing campaign.
question: What is required under GDPR Art. 5 regarding the purposes for which personal data are processed?
option_a: They must be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes, but further processing is allowed for any additional purposes.
option_b: They must be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes.
option_c: They must be collected for unspecified purposes and can be further processed as needed.
option_d: They must be collected for purposes other than those specified, but with the consent of the data subject.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 5(b), personal data must be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes.

scenario: A public authority in Germany is processing personal data for a purpose other than that for which the data were collected.
question: What must the public authority in Germany do to ascertain whether the processing for another purpose is compatible with the purpose for which the data were collected?
option_a: Consult with the EU Data Protection Board
option_b: Take into account any link between the purposes for which the personal data have been collected and the purposes of the intended further processing
option_c: Notify the German Data Protection Authority
option_d: Seek consent from the data subject
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 6(4), the controller shall take into account, inter alia, any link between the purposes for which the personal data have been collected and the purposes of the intended further processing.

scenario: A company in France is processing personal data for a task carried out in the public interest.
question: What must the legal basis for the processing contain?
option_a: A general provision to adapt the application of rules of this Regulation
option_b: The types of data which are subject to the processing; the data subjects concerned; the entities to, and the purposes for which, the personal data may be disclosed
option_c: A provision to adapt the application of rules of this Regulation, inter alia, the general conditions governing the lawfulness of processing by the controller
option_d: A provision to adapt the application of rules of this Regulation, inter alia, the storage periods
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 6(3), the legal basis for the processing shall contain, inter alia, the types of data which are subject to the processing; the data subjects concerned; the entities to, and the purposes for which, the personal data may be disclosed

scenario: A bank in Germany needs to demonstrate that a customer has given consent to process their personal data.
question: What is the bank required to be able to demonstrate?
option_a: That the customer has signed a contract
option_b: That the customer has given consent to processing of their personal data
option_c: That the customer has been informed about the data protection officer
option_d: That the customer has paid a fee
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 7(1), the controller shall be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented to processing of their personal data.

scenario: A travel agency in France is collecting personal data from a customer for a booking.
question: What right does the customer have regarding their consent?
option_a: The right to access the data
option_b: The right to withdraw their consent at any time
option_c: The right to transfer the data to another agency
option_d: The right to delete the data
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 7(3), the data subject shall have the right to withdraw their consent at any time.

scenario: A company in Germany offers information society services to a 14-year-old child.
question: What is the minimum age for a child to provide consent for the processing of their personal data?
option_a: 13 years old
option_b: 16 years old
option_c: 18 years old
option_d: 21 years old
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 8, the processing of the personal data of a child shall be lawful where the child is at least 16 years old.

scenario: A French company offers information society services to a child.
question: What must the company do to verify consent for the processing of the child's personal data?
option_a: Verify the child's age
option_b: Make reasonable efforts to verify that consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility
option_c: Check the child's ID document
option_d: Contact the child's parents directly
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 8, the controller shall make reasonable efforts to verify in such cases that consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility over the child.

scenario: A German foundation in Germany processes special categories of personal data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person.
question: What is the lawful basis for processing genetic data for uniquely identifying a natural person?
option_a: Explicit consent from the data subject
option_b: Necessary for the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person
option_c: Necessary for the purposes of carrying out the obligations and exercising specific rights of the controller
option_d: Necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 9(1), processing of genetic data for uniquely identifying a natural person is prohibited, but paragraph 2(c) allows processing when necessary to protect the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person.

scenario: A French health professional in France processes special categories of personal data for medical diagnosis.
question: What is the condition under which a health professional can process special categories of personal data for medical diagnosis?
option_a: The data subject has given explicit consent to the processing
option_b: The data is processed by or under the responsibility of a professional subject to the obligation of professional secrecy under Union or Member State law
option_c: The data is processed in the course of its legitimate activities with appropriate safeguards by a foundation, association or any other not-for-profit body
option_d: The data is necessary for the purposes of carrying out the obligations and exercising specific rights of the controller
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 9(3), personal data referred to in paragraph 1 may be processed for the purposes referred to in point (h) of paragraph 2 when those data are processed by or under the responsibility of a professional subject to the obligation of professional secrecy under Union or Member State law.

scenario: A public authority in Germany is processing personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences.
question: Who is responsible for ensuring that the processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences is carried out in accordance with the law?
option_a: The Data Protection Officer
option_b: The Data Controller
option_c: The Supervisory Authority
option_d: The Data Subject
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 10, the data controller shall ensure that the processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences is carried out in accordance with the law.

scenario: A private company in France is processing personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences.
question: What is the purpose of processing personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences?
option_a: To protect the rights of the data subject
option_b: To prevent and investigate criminal offences
option_c: To provide employment opportunities
option_d: To sell personal data to third parties
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 10, the processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences or related security measures shall be carried out only by persons authorized to access them and shall be subject to the obligation of professional secrecy.

scenario: A small business in Germany wants to process personal data without identifying the data subject.
question: What is the controller required to do if the purposes for which it processes personal data do not require identification of the data subject?
option_a: Maintain additional information to identify the data subject.
option_b: Not be obliged to maintain, acquire or process additional information to identify the data subject.
option_c: Notify the supervisory authority about the data processing.
option_d: Provide information to the data subject about the processing.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 11, the controller shall not be obliged to maintain, acquire or process additional information in order to identify the data subject for the sole purpose of complying with this Regulation.

scenario: A data subject in France wants to exercise their rights under Articles 15 to 20.
question: When can Articles 15 to 20 apply to a data subject?
option_a: When the controller is able to identify the data subject.
option_b: When the data subject provides additional information enabling their identification.
option_c: When the data subject is a citizen of an EU country.
option_d: When the data subject is a minor.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 11, Articles 15 to 20 shall not apply except where the data subject, for the purpose of exercising his or her rights under those articles, provides additional information enabling his or her identification.

scenario: A company in Germany is required to provide information to a customer about their data processing.
question: How should the company provide the information to the customer?
option_a: In a complex, technical document
option_b: In a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language
option_c: Only orally, without any written record
option_d: Only through a third-party service provider
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 12, the controller shall provide any information in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language.

scenario: A public authority in France is asked by a citizen to provide information about their data processing.
question: What should the public authority do when the citizen requests the information orally?
option_a: Refuse to provide the information
option_b: Provide the information orally, provided that the identity of the citizen is proven by other means
option_c: Provide the information in writing only
option_d: Charge a fee for the information
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 12, when requested by the data subject, the information may be provided orally, provided that the identity of the data subject is proven by other means.

scenario: A German bank in Germany is collecting personal data from a customer for a loan application...
question: What information must the bank provide to the customer at the time when personal data are obtained?
option_a: The bank's financial reports for the past 5 years
option_b: The purposes of the processing for which the personal data are intended as well as the legal basis for the processing
option_c: The contact details of the bank's competitors
option_d: The customer's credit score for the past 3 months
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 13(c), the bank must provide the purposes of the processing for which the personal data are intended as well as the legal basis for the processing

scenario: A French company is collecting personal data from employees for HR purposes...
question: What right does the employee have regarding the storage of their personal data?
option_a: The right to request the company to delete the data immediately
option_b: The right to request access to and rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing concerning the data subject
option_c: The right to transfer the data to any other company
option_d: The right to request the company to store the data indefinitely
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 13(2)(a), the employee has the right to request access to and rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing concerning the data subject

scenario: A controller in Germany is required to inform a data subject about their right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority.
question: What is the time frame within which a controller must provide the data subject with the information referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 of GDPR Art. 14?
option_a: Within one week after obtaining the personal data
option_b: Within a reasonable period after obtaining the personal data, but at the latest within one month
option_c: At the time of the first communication to the data subject
option_d: When the personal data are first disclosed to another recipient
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 14(3)(a), the controller must provide the information within a reasonable period after obtaining the personal data, but at the latest within one month.

scenario: A company in France has appointed a data protection officer and wants to inform the data subject about their contact details.
question: Where must the controller provide the contact details of the data protection officer?
option_a: On the company's website
option_b: In the data protection policy document
option_c: In the first communication to the data subject
option_d: In the data subject's contract
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 14(1)(b), the controller must provide the contact details of the data protection officer, where applicable.

scenario: A French citizen requests access to their personal data from a French bank
question: What is the bank required to provide to the citizen upon request?
option_a: The bank's financial statements for the past year
option_b: The purposes of the processing, categories of personal data concerned, and the envisaged period for which the personal data will be stored
option_c: The bank's customer database for the entire EU
option_d: A list of all the bank's employees
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 15(1)(a), (b), and (d), the bank must provide the purposes of the processing, categories of personal data concerned, and the envisaged period for which the personal data will be stored

scenario: A German company receives a request from an employee for access to their personal data
question: How many copies of the personal data the company can charge the employee for?
option_a: One free copy and two paid copies
option_b: One free copy and any additional copies requested by the employee
option_c: Two free copies and any additional copies requested by the employee
option_d: No copies can be charged
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 15(3), the controller may charge a reasonable fee based on administrative costs for any further copies requested by the data subject

scenario: A consumer in Germany seeks to correct inaccurate information in their credit report.
question: What is the timeframe for a data subject to obtain rectification of inaccurate personal data under GDPR?
option_a: Immediately
option_b: Without undue delay
option_c: Within 30 days
option_d: Upon request from the controller
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 16, the data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller without undue delay the rectification of inaccurate personal data concerning him or her.

scenario: A company in France wants to rectify its employee's incomplete personal data.
question: What is the purpose-based right of a data subject under GDPR Art. 16?
option_a: To delete the personal data
option_b: To have incomplete personal data completed
option_c: To restrict the processing of personal data
option_d: To transfer the personal data to another controller
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 16, taking into account the purposes of the processing, the data subject shall have the right to have incomplete personal data completed, including by means of providing a supplementary statement.

scenario: A German citizen in Germany requests the erasure of personal data stored by a company.
question: What is the timeframe for the controller to erase personal data under GDPR Art. 17?
option_a: Within 30 days
option_b: Without undue delay
option_c: Within 1 year
option_d: Within 6 months
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 17, the controller shall erase personal data without undue delay.

scenario: A French company is processing personal data for marketing purposes.
question: What ground can a data subject use to request erasure of personal data if they withdraw consent?
option_a: The personal data are no longer necessary for the purposes of the processing
option_b: The data subject withdraws consent on which the processing is based according to point (a) of Article 6(1), or point (a) of Article 9(2), and there is no other legal ground for the processing
option_c: The personal data have been unlawfully processed
option_d: The data subject objects to the processing pursuant to Article 21(1)
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 17(b), the data subject withdraws consent on which the processing is based according to point (a) of Article 6(1), or point (a) of Article 9(2), and where there is no other legal ground for the processing

scenario: A French citizen in France contests the accuracy of their personal data stored by a bank.
question: What can a data subject do if they contest the accuracy of their personal data?
option_a: Request erasure of the data
option_b: Obtain restriction of processing for a period enabling the controller to verify the accuracy of the data
option_c: Sue the bank for data protection violations
option_d: Demand access to the data
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 18(a), the data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller restriction of processing where the accuracy of the personal data is contested by the data subject, for a period enabling the controller to verify the accuracy of the data.

scenario: A German company receives a request from a customer to restrict the processing of their data.
question: What can the company do with the restricted data?
option_a: Sell the data to a third party
option_b: Process the data only with the data subject's consent or for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims
option_c: Share the data with the supervisory authority
option_d: Delete the data immediately
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 18(2), where processing has been restricted under paragraph 1, such personal data shall, with the exception of storage, only be processed with the data subject's consent or for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims...

scenario: A French company, 'EcoFrance', discloses personal data to a third-party processor in the UK.
question: What must EcoFrance communicate to the third-party processor?
option_a: A rectification of personal data
option_b: A rectification, erasure, or restriction of processing of personal data
option_c: An erasure of personal data
option_d: A restriction of processing of personal data
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 19, EcoFrance must communicate a rectification, erasure, or restriction of processing of personal data to the third-party processor.

scenario: A German startup, 'GreenTech', discloses personal data to a third-party recipient in the EU.
question: What must GreenTech inform the data subject about if requested?
option_a: The third-party recipient's contact information
option_b: Those recipients to whom the personal data have been disclosed
option_c: The data subject's rights under GDPR
option_d: The data subject's data protection officer
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 19, GreenTech must inform the data subject about those recipients to whom the personal data have been disclosed if the data subject requests it.

scenario: A German citizen, Herr Müller, wants to transfer his personal data from a German bank to a new bank in the EU.
question: What is the basis for the right to data portability under GDPR?
option_a: The processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest.
option_b: The processing is based on consent pursuant to point (a) of Article 6(1) or point (a) of Article 9(2) or on a contract pursuant to point (b) of Article 6(1)
option_c: The processing is carried out by manual means.
option_d: The data subject has objected to the processing.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 20, the right to data portability applies when the processing is based on consent pursuant to point (a) of Article 6(1) or point (a) of Article 9(2) or on a contract pursuant to point (b) of Article 6(1)

scenario: A French company, Le Coeur de la Vie, wants to transfer a customer's personal data to a new CRM system.
question: Can the data subject transmit the data directly from one controller to another under GDPR?
option_a: The data subject must request the data in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format.
option_b: The data subject shall have the right to have the personal data transmitted directly from one controller to another, where technically feasible.
option_c: The data subject must pay a fee for the data transfer.
option_d: The data subject must provide additional personal data to the new controller.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 20(2), the data subject shall have the right to have the personal data transmitted directly from one controller to another, where technically feasible.

scenario: A German consumer in Germany objects to processing of their personal data for direct marketing purposes.
question: How does the data subject object to processing of their personal data for direct marketing purposes?
option_a: By writing a letter to the controller
option_b: By automated means using technical specifications
option_c: By filing a complaint with the supervisory authority
option_d: By making a phone call to the controller
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 21(5), the data subject may exercise their right to object by automated means using technical specifications.

scenario: A French company processes personal data for scientific research purposes.
question: What happens to the personal data when the data subject objects to processing for scientific research purposes?
option_a: The data is deleted immediately
option_b: The data is no longer processed
option_c: The data is anonymized
option_d: The data is stored for 5 years
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 21(1), the controller shall no longer process the personal data unless the controller demonstrates compelling legitimate grounds for the processing which override the interests, rights and freedoms of the data subject.

scenario: A bank in Germany needs to implement measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests.
question: What is required by the bank in Germany?
option_a: Suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests
option_b: Human intervention on the part of the controller
option_c: Data protection officer appointment
option_d: Data subject's explicit consent
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 22(3), the data controller shall implement suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests, at least the right to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller.

scenario: A French company wants to use automated processing to make decisions about its customers.
question: What right does the data subject have?
option_a: The right to access personal data
option_b: The right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing
option_c: The right to erasure personal data
option_d: The right to data portability
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 22(1), the data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling.

scenario: A Member State in Germany introduces a legislative measure to restrict data subject rights in the context of a public security threat.
question: What must a legislative measure under GDPR Art. 23 contain, at least, regarding the scope of the restrictions introduced?
option_a: The name of the data protection officer
option_b: The scope of the restrictions introduced
option_c: The categories of personal data processed
option_d: The storage periods of the data
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 23, any legislative measure shall contain specific provisions at least as to the scope of the restrictions introduced.

scenario: A company in France is subject to a legislative measure restricting the processing of personal data for national security purposes.
question: What is the purpose of the processing or categories of processing that a legislative measure under GDPR Art. 23 must specify?
option_a: The risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects
option_b: The purposes of the processing or categories of processing
option_c: The storage periods of the data
option_d: The categories of controllers
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 23, any legislative measure shall contain specific provisions at least as to the purposes of the processing or categories of processing.

scenario: A large retail company in Germany needs to implement measures to ensure data protection.
question: What should the company implement to ensure data protection?
option_a: Approved codes of conduct as referred to in Article 40
option_b: Appropriate technical and organisational measures
option_c: Data protection policies by the controller
option_d: Certification mechanisms as referred to in Article 42
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 24(1), the controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure and to be able to demonstrate that processing is performed in accordance with this Regulation.

scenario: A small startup in France needs to review its data protection measures.
question: How often should the measures implemented by the startup be reviewed?
option_a: Every 5 years
option_b: Where necessary
option_c: Every 10 years
option_d: Every 2 years
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 24(1), those measures shall be reviewed and updated where necessary.

scenario: A controller in France is planning to implement data protection measures for a new project.
question: According to GDPR, what should the controller implement at the time of determining the means for processing?
option_a: A data protection impact assessment
option_b: Appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as pseudonymisation
option_c: A data protection officer
option_d: A data protection audit
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 25(1), the controller should implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as pseudonymisation, which are designed to implement data-protection principles, such as data minimisation, in an effective manner.

scenario: A small business in Germany is collecting personal data from customers for a loyalty programme.
question: What is required by default when collecting personal data under GDPR?
option_a: To make personal data accessible to an indefinite number of natural persons
option_b: To process only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing
option_c: To pseudonymise all personal data collected
option_d: To store personal data for a maximum of one year
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 25(2), the controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed.

scenario: A multinational corporation in Germany is processing personal data jointly with a German subsidiary.
question: What must the arrangement between the joint controllers in Germany reflect?
option_a: The respective roles and relationships of the joint controllers vis-à-vis the data subjects and the exercising of the rights of the data subject.
option_b: The essence of the arrangement and the respective roles and relationships of the joint controllers vis-à-vis the data subjects.
option_c: The exercising of the rights of the data subject and their respective duties to provide the information referred to in Articles 13 and 14.
option_d: The respective roles and relationships of the joint controllers vis-à-vis the data subjects and the exercising of the rights of the data subject.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 26(2), the arrangement shall duly reflect the respective roles and relationships of the joint controllers vis-à-vis the data subjects.

scenario: A company in France is processing personal data jointly with a French non-profit organization.
question: How can a data subject exercise his or her rights under the GDPR?
option_a: Only against one of the controllers.
option_b: Irrespective of the terms of the arrangement, the data subject may exercise his or her rights under this Regulation in respect of and against each of the controllers.
option_c: Only against the controller that initiated the data processing.
option_d: Only against the controller that is subject to EU law.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 26(3), the data subject may exercise his or her rights under this Regulation in respect of and against each of the controllers.

scenario: A company in Germany offering goods or services to data subjects in France
question: Where should a representative be established, if a company is offering goods or services to data subjects in a country other than where the company is based?
option_a: In the country where the company is based
option_b: In one of the Member States where the data subjects are
option_c: In the EU headquarters
option_d: In the country where the supervisory authority is located
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 27(3), the representative shall be established in one of the Member States where the data subjects, whose personal data are processed in relation to the offering of goods or services to them, or whose behaviour is monitored, are.

scenario: A small startup in the UK processing occasional personal data
question: What type of processing is exempt from the obligation to designate a representative in the Union?
option_a: Processing which is occasional, includes special categories of data and is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons
option_b: Processing which is occasional, does not include special categories of data and is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons
option_c: Processing which is frequent, includes special categories of data and is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons
option_d: Processing which is occasional, includes special categories of data and is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 27(2)(a), the obligation laid down in paragraph 1 of this Article shall not apply to processing which is occasional, does not include, on a large scale, processing of special categories of data as referred to in Article 9(1) or processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10, and is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.

scenario: A controller in Germany hires a processor to process personal data of EU citizens.
question: What is required of the processor in the contract with the controller?
option_a: To process the data without informing the controller.
option_b: To process the data only on documented instructions from the controller.
option_c: To store the data indefinitely.
option_d: To share the data with other processors without permission.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 28(3)(a), the processor must process the personal data only on documented instructions from the controller.

scenario: A processor in France is hired by a controller to process sensitive personal data of EU citizens.
question: What is the processor's responsibility regarding the controller's obligations to respond to data subject requests?
option_a: To ignore the controller's requests.
option_b: To assist the controller by appropriate technical and organisational measures.
option_c: To respond to the data subjects directly.
option_d: To delete the data without informing the controller.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 28(5), the processor must assist the controller by appropriate technical and organisational measures, insofar as this is possible, for the fulfilment of the controller's obligation to respond to requests for exercising the data subject's rights.

scenario: A data processor in Germany is working with a client in France.
question: Who is allowed to process personal data under GDPR Art. 29?
option_a: Only the data controller
option_b: The processor and any person acting under the authority of the controller or of the processor
option_c: Only the data subject
option_d: The data protection officer
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 29, the processor and any person acting under the authority of the controller or of the processor are allowed to process personal data.

scenario: A company in Italy is processing personal data under a contract.
question: Who must give instructions for the processing of personal data under GDPR Art. 29?
option_a: The data protection officer
option_b: The data controller
option_c: The data processor
option_d: The supervisory authority
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 29, the controller must give instructions for the processing of personal data.

scenario: A small business in France needs to maintain records of processing activities.
question: Who is required to maintain a record of processing activities under GDPR Art. 30?
option_a: The data protection officer only
option_b: The controller and, where applicable, the controller's representative
option_c: The supervisory authority only
option_d: The data protection officer and the supervisory authority
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 30, the controller and, where applicable, the controller's representative shall maintain a record of processing activities.

scenario: A large corporation in Germany is processing personal data.
question: What should the record of processing activities contain under GDPR Art. 30?
option_a: A description of the categories of recipients to whom the personal data have been or will be disclosed
option_b: The purposes of the processing and a description of the categories of data subjects and of the categories of personal data
option_c: The categories of data subjects only
option_d: The categories of recipients to whom the personal data have been or will be disclosed only
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 30, the record shall contain all of the following information: the purposes of the processing; (c) a description of the categories of data subjects and of the categories of personal data;

scenario: A data processor in Germany is requested to cooperate with the supervisory authority in the performance of its tasks.
question: Who is required to cooperate with the supervisory authority under GDPR?
option_a: The data controller only
option_b: The controller and the processor and their representatives
option_c: The data subject only
option_d: The supervisory authority only
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 31, the controller and the processor and, where applicable, their representatives, shall cooperate with the supervisory authority in the performance of its tasks.

scenario: A data controller in France is performing tasks with the supervisory authority.
question: Who is required to cooperate with the supervisory authority in the performance of its tasks?
option_a: The data processor only
option_b: The controller and the processor and their representatives
option_c: The data controller only
option_d: The data subject and the processor
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 31, the controller and the processor and, where applicable, their representatives, shall cooperate with the supervisory authority in the performance of its tasks.

scenario: A small startup in France needs to ensure the security of its customer data.
question: What should the startup implement to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk?
option_a: The ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services only during weekdays.
option_b: The ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
option_c: A process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the security of the processing only for the first year.
option_d: The pseudonymisation and encryption of personal data only for employees.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 32, the controller and the processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including inter alia as appropriate: (b) the ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.

scenario: A German company is processing personal data of its employees.
question: Who can process personal data without instructions from the controller?
option_a: A natural person acting under the authority of the processor who has access to personal data.
option_b: A natural person acting under the authority of the controller or the processor who has access to personal data.
option_c: A natural person acting under the authority of the controller who has access to personal data and is required to do so by Union law.
option_d: A natural person acting under the authority of the processor who has access to personal data and is required to do so by Union or Member State law.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 32(4), the controller and processor shall take steps to ensure that any natural person acting under the authority of the controller or the processor who has access to personal data does not process them except on instructions from the controller, unless he or she is required to do so by Union or Member State law.

scenario: A German bank in Germany experiences a personal data breach and needs to notify the supervisory authority.
question: How long does a controller have to notify the supervisory authority after becoming aware of a personal data breach?
option_a: Within 24 hours
option_b: Within 72 hours
option_c: Within 1 week
option_d: Within 30 days
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 33(1), the controller shall notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it.

scenario: A French e-commerce company is required to notify the supervisory authority about a personal data breach.
question: What information must the controller include in the notification to the supervisory authority?
option_a: Only the name of the data protection officer
option_b: The name and contact details of the data protection officer or other contact point where more information can be obtained
option_c: The categories and approximate number of data subjects concerned and the categories and approximate number of personal data records concerned only
option_d: The name of the supervisory authority only
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 33(3), the notification to the supervisory authority shall at least describe the nature of the personal data breach including where possible, the categories and approximate number of data subjects concerned and the categories and approximate number of personal data records concerned, and communicate the name and contact details of the data protection officer or other contact point where more information can be obtained.

scenario: A small startup in Germany discovers a personal data breach affecting 100 customers.
question: When must a personal data breach be communicated to the data subject?
option_a: Immediately, regardless of the risk level.
option_b: When the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
option_c: Only if the breach affects more than 1000 customers.
option_d: When the breach is discovered in a EU country other than Germany.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 34(1), the controller shall communicate the personal data breach to the data subject when the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.

scenario: A large corporation in France is considering whether to inform its customers about a data breach.
question: Under what conditions is the controller not required to inform the data subject directly?
option_a: If the breach affects only employees.
option_b: If the controller has implemented appropriate technical and organisational protection measures.
option_c: If the breach is minor and affects only 10 customers.
option_d: If the breach occurred before the GDPR came into effect.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 34(3), the controller is not required to inform the data subject directly if the controller has implemented appropriate technical and organisational protection measures.

scenario: A controller in Germany wants to conduct a data protection impact assessment.
question: Who should the controller seek advice from when carrying out a data protection impact assessment?
option_a: The supervisory authority
option_b: The data protection officer, where designated
option_c: The data subject
option_d: The board referred to in Article 68
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 35(2), the controller shall seek the advice of the data protection officer, where designated, when carrying out a data protection impact assessment.

scenario: A company in France wants to process a large scale of personal data relating to criminal convictions.
question: What is required prior to the processing of the envisaged operations?
option_a: A data protection impact assessment is not required
option_b: A data protection impact assessment shall be carried out
option_c: A review of the data protection impact assessment is required
option_d: A compliance report is submitted to the supervisory authority
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 35(3)(b), processing on a large scale of special categories of data referred to in Article 9(1), or of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10, requires a data protection impact assessment prior to the processing of the envisaged operations.

scenario: A German bank in Germany wants to process customer data and needs to consult the supervisory authority prior to processing.
question: What is the maximum period for the supervisory authority to provide written advice to the controller?
option_a: 4 weeks
option_b: up to eight weeks
option_c: 12 weeks
option_d: six months
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 36, the supervisory authority shall provide written advice to the controller within a period of up to eight weeks of receipt of the request for consultation.

scenario: A French company is preparing a proposal for a legislative measure to be adopted by the French parliament.
question: Who must consult the supervisory authority during the preparation of a proposal for a legislative measure?
option_a: The data protection officer
option_b: Member States
option_c: The controller
option_d: The processor
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 36, Member States shall consult the supervisory authority during the preparation of a proposal for a legislative measure to be adopted by a national parliament.

scenario: A public authority in Germany is required to designate a data protection officer.
question: What is the minimum requirement for a public authority to designate a data protection officer?
option_a: A data protection officer is required if the public authority processes special categories of data.
option_b: A data protection officer is required if the public authority consists of processing operations which, by virtue of their nature, their scope and/or their purposes, require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale.
option_c: A data protection officer is required if the public authority processes personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences.
option_d: A data protection officer is required if the public authority is a group of undertakings.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 37, a data protection officer is required in any case where the processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except for courts acting in their judicial capacity.

scenario: A large e-commerce company in France wants to designate a data protection officer.
question: Can a group of undertakings appoint a single data protection officer?
option_a: No, a group of undertakings must appoint a data protection officer for each establishment.
option_b: Yes, provided that a data protection officer is easily accessible from each establishment.
option_c: Yes, if the group of undertakings processes special categories of data.
option_d: Yes, if the group of undertakings is a public authority.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 37, a group of undertakings may appoint a single data protection officer provided that a data protection officer is easily accessible from each establishment.

scenario: A medium-sized enterprise in Germany is hiring a new data protection officer.
question: According to GDPR Art. 38, what must the controller and processor ensure?
option_a: The data protection officer is solely responsible for data protection compliance.
option_b: The data protection officer is involved in all issues which relate to the protection of personal data.
option_c: The data protection officer must report directly to the EU Commission.
option_d: The data protection officer is only responsible for data processing operations.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 38(1), the controller and processor must ensure that the data protection officer is involved, properly and in a timely manner, in all issues which relate to the protection of personal data.

scenario: A small non-profit organization in France is setting up a data protection framework.
question: According to GDPR Art. 38, what must the controller and processor provide to the data protection officer?
option_a: A 5-year contract.
option_b: Support in performing the tasks referred to in the regulation.
option_c: A 10,000 Euro budget.
option_d: A 2-year training program.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 38(2), the controller and processor shall support the data protection officer in performing the tasks referred to in the regulation.

scenario: A medium-sized company in Germany needs to inform its employees about their obligations under the GDPR.
question: What is one of the tasks of the data protection officer?
option_a: To perform data protection impact assessments only
option_b: To inform and advise the controller or processor and the employees who carry out processing of their obligations pursuant to this Regulation
option_c: To monitor compliance with the GDPR only
option_d: To provide advice on data subject rights only
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 39(a), the data protection officer shall inform and advise the controller or the processor and the employees who carry out processing of their obligations pursuant to this Regulation

scenario: A public administration in France needs to determine the tasks of its data protection officer.
question: What is one of the tasks of the data protection officer?
option_a: To provide advice on data protection impact assessments and to perform audits only
option_b: To monitor compliance with this Regulation, with other Union or Member State data protection provisions and with the policies of the controller or processor in relation to the protection of personal data
option_c: To inform and advise the controller or processor only
option_d: To consult with the supervisory authority only
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 39(b), the data protection officer shall monitor compliance with this Regulation, with other Union or Member State data protection provisions and with the policies of the controller or processor in relation to the protection of personal data

scenario: A supervisory authority in France wants to approve a code of conduct for a specific sector.
question: Who must be consulted before approving a draft code of conduct that relates to processing activities in several Member States?
option_a: The European Data Protection Board
option_b: The Commission and the European Data Protection Board
option_c: The European Commission alone
option_d: The Article 29 Working Party
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 40(7), the supervisory authority shall submit the draft code to the Board before approving it.

scenario: A company in Germany wants to adhere to a code of conduct.
question: Who can adhere to a code of conduct approved by the Commission?
option_a: Only controllers subject to the GDPR
option_b: Controllers or processors that are not subject to the GDPR
option_c: Only data protection officers
option_d: Only processors that are subject to the GDPR
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 40(3), controllers or processors that are not subject to the GDPR can adhere to a code of conduct approved by the Commission.

scenario: A supervisory authority in Germany wants to accredit a body to monitor compliance with a code of conduct.
question: What must a body have to be accredited to monitor compliance with a code of conduct?
option_a: Demonstrated its independence and expertise in relation to the subject-matter of the code to the satisfaction of the supervisory authority.
option_b: Established procedures which allow it to assess the eligibility of controllers and processors concerned to apply the code, to monitor their compliance with its provisions and to periodically review its operation.
option_c: Demonstrated to the satisfaction of the supervisory authority that its tasks and duties do not result in a conflict of interests.
option_d: Established procedures and structures to handle complaints about infringements of the code or the manner in which the code has been, or is being, implemented by a controller or processor.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 41(2), a body must establish procedures which allow it to assess the eligibility of controllers and processors concerned to apply the code, to monitor their compliance with its provisions and to periodically review its operation.

scenario: A supervisory authority in France wants to revoke the accreditation of a body that has been monitoring compliance with a code of conduct.
question: Under what circumstances can a supervisory authority revoke the accreditation of a body?
option_a: If the body has demonstrated its independence and expertise in relation to the subject-matter of the code.
option_b: If the conditions for accreditation are not, or are no longer, met.
option_c: If the body has established procedures which allow it to assess the eligibility of controllers and processors concerned to apply the code.
option_d: If the body has taken actions that do not infringe the Regulation.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 41(5), the supervisory authority shall revoke the accreditation of a body if the conditions for accreditation are not, or are no longer, met.

scenario: A supervisory authority in Germany is considering establishing data protection certification mechanisms.
question: Who approves the criteria for certification?
option_a: The European Commission
option_b: The competent supervisory authority
option_c: The European Data Protection Board
option_d: The European Parliament
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 42, a certification pursuant to this Article shall be issued by the certification bodies referred to in Article 43 or by the competent supervisory authority, on the basis of criteria approved by that competent supervisory authority.

scenario: A small enterprise in France wants to demonstrate compliance with the GDPR.
question: What type of entities can establish data protection certification mechanisms?
option_a: Only large enterprises
option_b: Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises
option_c: Only controllers subject to the GDPR
option_d: Only processors subject to the GDPR
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 42, the specific needs of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises shall be taken into account.

scenario: A certification body in Germany is seeking accreditation under GDPR.
question: To be accredited, a certification body must be accredited by which of the following?
option_a: The EU Commission
option_b: The national accreditation body named in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 or the supervisory authority
option_c: The European Data Protection Board
option_d: The European Parliament
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 43(1)(a) and (b), a certification body must be accredited by one or both of the national accreditation body or the supervisory authority.

scenario: A certification body in the UK has been accredited by the national accreditation body.
question: What must the certification body have demonstrated to the satisfaction of the competent supervisory authority for accreditation?
option_a: That their tasks and duties do not result in a conflict of interests and they have a maximum of 3 employees
option_b: That their tasks and duties do not result in a conflict of interests, they have expertise in relation to data protection, and they have undertaken to respect the criteria referred to in Article 42(5)
option_c: That they have a maximum of 5 years of experience in data protection
option_d: That they have a budget of €100,000 for data protection
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 43(2)(a), (b), (d), and (e), a certification body must demonstrate that their tasks and duties do not result in a conflict of interests, they have expertise in relation to data protection, and they have undertaken to respect the criteria referred to in Article 42(5).

scenario: A German bank in Germany is considering transferring personal data to a company in the United States.
question: What must be complied with by the controller and processor before transferring personal data to a third country?
option_a: The Data Protection Officer's approval
option_b: The conditions laid down in Chapter of this Regulation
option_c: The Supervisory Authority's consent
option_d: The EU Commission's permission
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 44, all provisions in this Chapter shall be applied to ensure the level of protection of natural persons guaranteed by this Regulation is not undermined.

scenario: A French company is planning to transfer personal data to a third country.
question: When can a transfer of personal data to a third country take place?
option_a: Only if the Data Subject gives explicit consent
option_b: If the conditions laid down in this Chapter are complied with by the controller and processor
option_c: After a 6-month notice period to the Supervisory Authority
option_d: When the EU Commission has given a prior approval
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 44, any transfer of personal data which are undergoing processing or are intended for processing after transfer to a third country or to an international organisation shall take place only if, subject to the other provisions of this Regulation, the conditions laid down in this Chapter are complied with by the controller and processor.

scenario: A company in France is planning to transfer personal data to a third country.
question: What is required for a transfer of personal data to a third country?
option_a: A specific authorisation from the Commission is required.
option_b: The Commission has decided that the third country ensures an adequate level of protection.
option_c: The company must comply with the General Data Protection Regulation.
option_d: The transfer must be approved by the French Data Protection Authority.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 45(1), a transfer of personal data to a third country may take place where the Commission has decided that the third country ensures an adequate level of protection.

scenario: The European Commission is considering adopting a decision on the adequacy of a third country.
question: How often must the Commission review the adequacy of the level of protection?
option_a: Every two years.
option_b: At least every four years.
option_c: Every six months.
option_d: Annually.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 45(3), the implementing act shall provide for a mechanism for a periodic review, at least every four years.

scenario: A German bank in Germany is considering transferring personal data to a company in the United States.
question: What is required for a German bank to transfer personal data to a company in the United States?
option_a: A legally binding and enforceable instrument between the bank and the company
option_b: Appropriate safeguards, and on condition that enforceable data subject rights and effective legal remedies for data subjects are available
option_c: A contract between the bank and the company
option_d: A certification from the German supervisory authority
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 46(1), appropriate safeguards, and on condition that enforceable data subject rights and effective legal remedies for data subjects are available

scenario: A French company is transferring personal data to a subsidiary in the United Kingdom.
question: How can the French company provide appropriate safeguards for the transfer of personal data to the UK subsidiary?
option_a: By obtaining a certification from the UK Information Commissioner's Office
option_b: By using standard data protection clauses adopted by the Commission in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 93(2)
option_c: By inserting provisions into the company's internal policies
option_d: By obtaining a contract with the UK subsidiary
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 46(2)(c), standard data protection clauses adopted by the Commission in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 93(2) can be used to provide appropriate safeguards

scenario: A multinational company in Germany needs to designate a data protection officer to monitor compliance with its binding corporate rules.
question: What tasks should the data protection officer be responsible for?
option_a: Conducting data protection audits and methods for ensuring corrective actions to protect the rights of the data subject.
option_b: Providing information on the binding corporate rules to the data subjects in addition to Articles 13 and 14.
option_c: Cooperating with the supervisory authority to ensure compliance by any member of the group of undertakings.
option_d: Fulfil the requirements laid down in paragraph 2 of GDPR Art. 47.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 47(j), the data protection officer should be responsible for monitoring compliance with the binding corporate rules, including data protection audits and methods for ensuring corrective actions to protect the rights of the data subject.

scenario: A UK-based subsidiary of a US parent company wants to transfer personal data to a third country.
question: What must the subsidiary specify in its binding corporate rules regarding data transfers?
option_a: The categories of personal data, the type of processing, and the purposes of the data transfer.
option_b: The categories of personal data, the type of processing, and the purposes of the data transfer, the type of data subjects affected, and the identification of the third country or countries in question.
option_c: The categories of personal data, the type of processing, and the purposes of the data transfer, and the type of data subjects affected.

scenario: A data subject in France requests access to documents submitted to the EU Board.
question: What regulation governs access to these documents?
option_a: Regulation (EC) No 1050/2001
option_b: Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001
option_c: Regulation (EC) No 1060/2001
option_d: Regulation (EU) No 1070/2016
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 76, access to documents submitted to members of the Board, experts and representatives of third parties shall be governed by Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001 of the European Parliament and of the Council.

scenario: A data subject in Germany considers that their personal data is being processed in a way that infringes the GDPR.
question: In which Member State can the data subject lodge a complaint?
option_a: The Member State of the controller's headquarters
option_b: The Member State of their habitual residence, place of work or place of the alleged infringement
option_c: The Member State of the supervisory authority's headquarters
option_d: The Member State where the data was collected
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 77(1), the data subject can lodge a complaint in the Member State of their habitual residence, place of work or place of the alleged infringement.

scenario: A data subject lodges a complaint with a supervisory authority in the EU.
question: What does the supervisory authority with which the complaint has been lodged inform the complainant about?
option_a: The possibility of a judicial remedy only
option_b: The progress and the outcome of the complaint including the possibility of a judicial remedy
option_c: The identity of the data controller
option_d: The complainant's right to erasure
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 77(2), the supervisory authority with which the complaint has been lodged shall inform the complainant on the progress and the outcome of the complaint including the possibility of a judicial remedy.

scenario: A data subject in Germany lodges a complaint with the German Data Protection Authority.
question: Where should proceedings be brought against a supervisory authority?
option_a: The courts of the Member State where the data subject resides.
option_b: The courts of the Member State where the supervisory authority is established.
option_c: The European Court of Justice.
option_d: The courts of the Member State where the complaint was lodged.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 78.3, proceedings against a supervisory authority shall be brought before the courts of the Member State where the supervisory authority is established.

scenario: A data subject in Spain files a complaint with the Spanish Data Protection Authority.
question: What is the timeframe within which the supervisory authority must inform the data subject on the progress or outcome of the complaint?
option_a: One month.
option_b: Three months.
option_c: Six months.
option_d: No specific timeframe is mentioned.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 78.2, the supervisory authority must inform the data subject within three months on the progress or outcome of the complaint.

scenario: A data subject in Germany considers that their rights under the GDPR have been infringed as a result of the processing of their personal data.
question: Where can proceedings against a controller or a processor be brought?
option_a: Before the European Court of Justice
option_b: Before the courts of the Member State where the controller or processor has an establishment
option_c: Before the courts of the Member State where the data subject has their habitual residence
option_d: Before the courts of the country of origin of the data subject
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 79(2), proceedings against a controller or a processor shall be brought before the courts of the Member State where the controller or processor has an establishment.

scenario: A data subject in France has a complaint against a controller in Italy.
question: Where can the data subject bring proceedings against the controller?
option_a: Before the courts of the Member State where the data subject has their habitual residence
option_b: Before the courts of the Member State where the controller has an establishment
option_c: Before the courts of the country of origin of the data subject
option_d: Before the European Court of Justice
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 79(2), proceedings against a controller or a processor shall be brought before the courts of the Member State where the controller or processor has an establishment.

scenario: A not-for-profit body in Germany wants to lodge a complaint on behalf of a data subject.
question: What is required for a not-for-profit body to lodge a complaint on behalf of a data subject?
option_a: The body must have a profit motive.
option_b: The body must be properly constituted in accordance with the law of a Member State.
option_c: The body must have a majority of non-profit members.
option_d: The body must be active in the field of animal rights.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 80, the body must be properly constituted in accordance with the law of a Member State.

scenario: A consumer association in France considers that the rights of a data subject under the GDPR have been infringed.
question: What right does the consumer association in France have?
option_a: To exercise the right to receive compensation referred to in Article 82 on behalf of the data subject.
option_b: To lodge a complaint with the supervisory authority which is competent pursuant to Article 77 and to exercise the rights referred to in Articles 78 and 79 on behalf of the data subject.
option_c: To exercise the right to be forgotten.
option_d: To exercise the right to data portability.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 80, the consumer association in France has the right to lodge a complaint with the supervisory authority which is competent pursuant to Article 77 and to exercise the rights referred to in Articles 78 and 79 on behalf of the data subject.

scenario: A court in France is informed of proceedings concerning the same subject matter as regards processing by the same controller.
question: What should the French court do?
option_a: Contact the court in the other Member State to confirm the existence of proceedings.
option_b: Contact the court in the other Member State to confirm the existence of proceedings.
option_c: Decline jurisdiction if the court first seized has jurisdiction over the actions in question.
option_d: Suspend its proceedings.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 81(1), where a competent court of a Member State has information on proceedings, concerning the same subject matter as regards processing by the same controller or processor, that are pending in a court in another Member State, it shall contact that court in the other Member State to confirm the existence of such proceedings.

scenario: A court in Germany is informed of proceedings concerning the same subject matter as regards processing by the same controller.
question: What should the German court do if proceedings are pending in a court in another Member State?
option_a: Decline jurisdiction if the court first seized has jurisdiction over the actions in question.
option_b: Suspend its proceedings.
option_c: Contact the court in the other Member State to confirm the existence of proceedings.
option_d: Proceed with its proceedings.
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 81(2), where proceedings concerning the same subject matter as regards processing of the same controller or processor are pending in a court in another Member State, any competent court other than the court first seized may suspend its proceedings.

scenario: A small business in Germany is involved in a data breach and is liable for the damage caused.
question: Who is liable for the damage caused by processing under GDPR Art. 82?
option_a: The data subject
option_b: The controller involved in processing
option_c: The supervisory authority
option_d: The processor who acted outside lawful instructions
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 82(2), any controller involved in processing shall be liable for the damage caused by processing which infringes this Regulation.

scenario: A multinational company with headquarters in France has multiple data processors involved in the same processing operation.
question: What happens if a controller or processor has paid full compensation for the damage suffered under GDPR Art. 82?
option_a: The controller or processor can claim back from the data subject
option_b: The controller or processor can claim back from the other controllers or processors involved in the same processing
option_c: The controller or processor must report the incident to the supervisory authority
option_d: The controller or processor is exempt from liability
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 82(5), where a controller or processor has, in accordance with paragraph 4, paid full compensation for the damage suffered, that controller or processor shall be entitled to claim back from the other controllers or processors involved in the same processing that part of the compensation corresponding to their part of responsibility for the damage, in accordance with the conditions set out in paragraph 2.

scenario: A German bank in Germany is fined for GDPR non-compliance. What must the supervisory authority consider when deciding on the amount of the administrative fine?
question: What factors should be taken into account?
option_a: Only the nature and gravity of the infringement
option_b: The nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, the intentional or negligent character of the infringement, and the degree of responsibility of the controller or processor
option_c: The number of data subjects affected and the level of damage suffered by them, and the degree of cooperation with the supervisory authority
option_d: The categories of personal data affected by the infringement and the manner in which the infringement became known to the supervisory authority
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 83(2), when deciding on the amount of the administrative fine, regard shall be given to the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, the intentional or negligent character of the infringement, and the degree of responsibility of the controller or processor.

scenario: A French company is fined for GDPR non-compliance. What can be imposed in addition to or instead of the administrative fine?
question: What measures can be taken?
option_a: Only measures referred to in points (a) to (h) and (j) of Article 58(2)
option_b: Measures referred to in points (a) to (h) and (j) of Article 58(2), and other penalties
option_c: Measures referred to in points (a) to (h) of Article 58(2), and fines referred to in points (i) and (k) of Article 58(2)
option_d: Measures referred to in points (i) and (j) of Article 58(2), and fines referred to in points (a) and (b) of Article 58(2)
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 83(2), administrative fines shall, depending on the circumstances of each individual case, be imposed in addition to, or instead of, measures referred to in points (a) to (h) and (j) of Article 58(2).

scenario: A Member State in Germany must notify the provisions of its law to the Commission by
question: What is the deadline for a Member State to notify the Commission about its law?
option_a: 15 June 2018
option_c: 31 December 2018
option_d: 1 January 2019
explanation: According to GDPR Art. 84, each Member State shall notify to the Commission the provisions of its law which it adopts pursuant to paragraph 1, by 25 May 2018

scenario: A company in France must ensure that its penalties are
question: What characteristics should penalties have?
option_a: proportional and dissuasive
option_b: effective, proportionate and dissuasive
option_c: only effective
option_d: only dissuasive
